extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers, researchers, and journal editors (scholarly/biomedical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the roles, methods, and evaluative criteria for manuscript peer review in academic journals, and recommendations for reviewer conduct and common reasons for acceptance or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review refers to the process through which scientific papers are evaluated by professionals in related academic fields. In scientific journals, peer review is used to determine whether a submitted paper is suitable for publication in terms of its scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review, distinctively characterized by horizontal evaluation by peers, is considered one of the fairest ways to assess the quality of papers; outcomes are a major determinant of whether articles are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review methods (single-blind / double-blind / open review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review methods vary from journal to journal, and can be generally divided into three methods: single-blind review, double-blind review, and open review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind review is a common practice, as it guarantees reviewers’ anonymity, enabling them to provide bold and candid reviews. In double-blind review, both the authors and the reviewers are anonymous, meaning that papers are evaluated based only on their academic value. Through blind review processes, journals can achieve an objective degree of fairness; most journals therefore use single- or double-blind review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-guided open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-guided open peer review is a method in which authors recommend professionals who will review their papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, papers undergo dynamic evaluations, high-quality reviews are provided, and collaboration between authors and reviewers can be encouraged. This review method can be especially useful if too few reviewers are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication review as an alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review has emerged as an alternative to traditional blind review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication review has received attention because blind review can be accompanied by delays, costs, difficulties in finding reviewers, reviewer load, bias, and plagiarism; post-publication review may help address some of these issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer primary roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer has two main roles. One is to evaluate the value of the paper for publication. The reviewer’s other role is to provide constructive criticism to the authors of the paper under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to international standards, evaluation options include 'accept,' 'accept pending revisions,' 'reconsider after major revisions,' and 'reject.' The reviewer advises the editor, who makes the final publication decision; cooperation between editor and reviewers promotes journal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to accept a manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Three reasons may cause a reviewer to agree to accept a paper: first, the paper is timely and relevant to the latest research trends; second, the paper is easy to read, logical, and well-written; and third, the research design and methods are scientifically reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These desiderata are useful for reviewers, researchers, and authors to be aware of when preparing or evaluating manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons to reject a manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers can be rejected for the following six reasons: (1) the paper is incomplete in terms of its statistical analysis; (2) the paper interprets results in an exaggerated way; (3) the methods are suboptimal or insufficiently described; (4) the sample size is too small; (5) the manuscript is written in a way that is too difficult to understand; and (6) there is an insufficient description of the paper’s limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should watch for these specific weaknesses when evaluating manuscripts (Bordage G. Reasons reviewers reject and accept manuscripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness in responding to review invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer should avoid replying too late about his or her choice to review a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays in responding to review invitations are a major reason for delaying the decision on a paper; prompt acceptance/decline helps maintain review timelines (the journal's process example: initial decision generally made within 3 weeks after reviewers decide whether to review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of reviews (avoid generic/noninformative reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of reviews should not be generic or noninformative. A review should include a critical analysis of the paper and its fundamental components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive, detailed criticism rather than cursory comments; the review should analyze study design, methods, statistics, interpretation, writing clarity, and limitations to be useful to authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer vs editor decision boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: The final decision on whether a paper is to be published is made by the journal’s editor or editorial board. The role of a reviewer is not to decide whether to publish a paper, but to advise the editor about the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should focus on objective evaluation and constructive feedback; cooperative collaboration between editor and reviewers enables publication of excellent papers and promotes improvements in journal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems and limitations of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems associated with the peer review process include delayed reviews, bias on the part of reviewers, and plagiarism. There are also challenges in finding reviewers and potential overload on certain reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these systemic issues when designing review processes or evaluating the trustworthiness of reviews; alternatives like author-guided open review and post-publication review are discussed as potential mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal procedural example: reviewer selection and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper review process of Archives of Craniofacial Surgery starts with submission; if judged appropriate, the editor selects three peer reviewers and the review process is conducted. The initial decision is generally made within 3 weeks after the reviewers decide whether to review the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of journal-level procedural expectations (select ~3 reviewers; aim for initial decisions within weeks) and can serve as a benchmark for timely review workflows.
